title: A Basket of Summer Fruit and a Famine of the Word
summary: In a fourth vision Amos sees a basket of summer fruit, and God announces that the end has come for Israel. Amos then exposes merchants who resent the Sabbath because it interrupts their cheating. God swears he will not forget, and he promises a day of darkness at noon, mourning like that for an only son, and a famine not of bread but of hearing the words of the LORD.
story: Chapter 7 ended with Amaziah trying to silence Amos and Amos announcing exile. The visions resume here with a fourth sight, built on a pun, and it confirms that the time for relenting is over. The rest of the chapter returns to the reasons: Amos brings back the charge he made at the very start (2:6-7) against those who trample the poor and sell the needy for a pair of sandals. The chapter moves the book toward its climax. God's people, who refused the prophets' word (2:12, 7:16), will one day search for that word and not find it. The fifth and final vision, in chapter 9, follows.
historical:
The setting is still the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II (about 793 to 753 BC), when trade flourished in the northern kingdom and wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. The judgment Amos announces came through Assyria within a generation, ending in the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. Verse 14 names three sanctuaries: Samaria, the capital; Dan, in the far north, where Jeroboam I had set up his second golden calf (1 Kings 12:29-30); and Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, an ancient site linked with Abraham and Isaac that northern Israelites evidently visited as pilgrims (compare 5:5).

Some interpreters have connected verse 9, the sun going down at noon, with a total solar eclipse that was visible in the region in 763 BC and was recorded in the Assyrian eponym lists (the lists naming each year after an official). That eclipse would have occurred in Amos's lifetime, and his hearers may have remembered it. The text does not say so directly, and darkness is also a common image for the Day of the LORD (5:18-20), so the connection is possible but not certain.
cultural:
Israel's calendar set aside the New Moon (the first day of each month) and the weekly Sabbath as days of rest from ordinary work, including trade (compare Nehemiah 13:15-22). The merchants in verse 5 keep these days outwardly but can hardly wait for them to end. Their cheating is double: they "reduce the ephah", using an undersized basket so the customer receives less grain, and "increase the shekel", using heavy weights so the customer pays more silver. Money in this period was weighed rather than coined, so crooked weights were a standard way to cheat. The Law forbade both (Leviticus 19:35-36, Deuteronomy 25:13-16).

To "buy the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals" (verse 6) probably refers to debt slavery: a poor family that could not repay even a small debt lost its members into servitude. "Selling even the chaff with the wheat" means selling the sweepings of the threshing floor as if they were grain. The mourning customs of verse 10, sackcloth and shaved heads, were the standard signs of grief, and mourning for an only son was the deepest grief a family could know, since it meant the end of the family's name.
literary: The vision turns on a wordplay. Summer fruit is qayits; the end is qets. The two words sounded almost the same, so the basket of ripe fruit becomes a sign that Israel is ripe for its end. The speech against the merchants (verses 4 to 6) lets them condemn themselves in their own words, quoting their impatient thoughts. God's oath in verse 7 is ironic: he swears "by the Pride of Jacob", which could mean by himself (the one who should be Jacob's pride) or by Jacob's arrogance, which is as unchanging as an oath. The rest of the chapter is a series of "in that day" and "the days are coming" sayings that describe the day of judgment through images of earthquake, flood, eclipse, mourning, and famine, ending with people staggering from sea to sea looking for a word from God.

outline.t: Fourth vision: a basket of summer fruit, the end has come
The merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end
God's oath: earthquake, darkness, and mourning
A famine of hearing the words of the LORD

doctrines.note: The Sabbath was meant as a gift of rest, and the laws on honest weights protected the poor. The merchants keep the forms and resent the purpose. Amos shows that God's law is concerned with the marketplace as much as the sanctuary.

The worst judgment in the chapter is not hunger for bread but the silence of God: "a famine of hearing the words of the LORD" (verse 11). A people who rejected God's word will find that it is not always available on demand.
God swears, "I will never forget any of their deeds" (verse 7). Judgment rests on God's full memory of wrongs done to the poor, even when the powerful have forgotten them.

words.note: Qayits, summer fruit. The late-summer harvest, especially figs, gathered at the end of the agricultural year. Its sound is close to qets, end, and the pun carries the vision's message: the harvest is in, the year is over, and Israel's time is up.

Qets, end. The word God speaks in verse 2, "The end has come". Later prophets use it for the end of an age or a time of judgment (Ezekiel 7:2-6 echoes this passage, and Daniel speaks of the time of the end).

Ra'av, famine or hunger. Famine was one of the covenant curses Israel feared most, and Amos 4:6 described famines God had already sent. Here the word is turned: the coming famine is of God's words. Physical hunger becomes a picture of spiritual abandonment.

christ: Two images from this chapter reappear at the cross. The Gospels record that darkness covered the land from noon until three in the afternoon while Jesus was crucified (Matthew 27:45, Mark 15:33), and Amos's picture of the sun going down at noon and of mourning "for an only son" gives that darkness its Old Testament weight. Zechariah 12:10 uses the same image of mourning for an only child, and John 19:37 applies Zechariah's passage to Jesus. The link is one of images and themes, not a direct prediction. The famine of the word also finds an answer: Jesus called himself the bread of life (John 6:35) and, quoting Deuteronomy, said people live by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). Where Amos foresaw silence, the New Testament announces that God has spoken in his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2).

hard.q: Would God really withhold his word from people who are seeking it?
hard.a: Verse 12 says people will seek the word of the LORD and not find it, which can sound as if God refuses sincere seekers. Read in context, the people who search are those who rejected the prophets when the word was plainly given (2:12, 7:12-16), and they look for it only when disaster strikes, as Saul sought a word from God after years of disobedience (1 Samuel 28:6). Many interpreters therefore read the famine as the consequence of a long refusal: those who silence God's messengers eventually find no messenger left. Others add that the seeking in verse 12 is frantic rather than repentant, a search for rescue rather than for God. The passage stands alongside many promises that those who seek God with all their heart will find him (Jeremiah 29:13), and it warns against assuming God's word will always be there to be picked up later.

questions: The merchants kept the Sabbath outwardly while resenting it. Where do you keep a religious form while your mind is on getting back to business?
Amos sees the cheating of the poor with weights and measures as a matter for God. What would honest weights look like in your work or spending?
What would it mean for you to experience a famine of hearing God's word, and what keeps you hungry for it now?
